Title: Evaluating the Energy Efficiency of Toubkal HPC: Insights for the Green500 Rankings and Its Metric

Abstract
Energy efficiency has emerged as a vital metric for evaluating high-
performance computing (HPC) systems, often measured by the
Green500 rankings using the "performance per watt" criterion. In
this paper, we assess the energy efficiency of the Toubkal Super-
computer based on the established Green500 metric. While we
acknowledge the notable advancements in the rankings, we argue
that the current energy efficiency metric for HPC systems adopted
by the Green500 community overlooks two critical factors: the in-
tegration of on-site renewable energy sources and the potential for
energy management through dynamic frequency scaling of proces-
sors. To support our argument, we consider GPU as well as dynamic
voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS) technologies in a series of ex-
periments. Utilizing our custom machine learning-based frequency
predictor, our findings clearly illustrate the significant potential
of energy management and DVFS to reduce energy consumption
without compromising operational performance.

center infrastructure designed to perform extensive and intricate

mathematical calculations efficiently. This capability is made possi-
ble by leveraging parallel resources, including a large number of
CPU cores and substantial memory. To evaluate and compare the
performance of different HPC systems, the scientific community,
including organizations like Top500 [8, 30], has adopted the FLOPS
metric. This metric measures the number of floating-point opera-
tions that an HPC system can execute in one second, serving as a
critical benchmark for performance.
The establishment of HPC infrastructure has become a source
of national pride for many countries, leading to significant invest-
ments from governments around the globe [19, 34]. These invest-
ments underscore the vital role that such advanced computational
resources play in advancing research and innovation in academia,
fostering breakthroughs across various scientific fields. For instance,
countries like China and the United States have made substantial
contributions to their HPC capabilities, recognizing that access to
powerful computing resources can accelerate discoveries in areas
such as climate modeling [16], genomics [13, 33], and AI [23].
Toubkal Supercomputer1 is an advanced HPC system meticu-
lously engineered to propel scientific research and foster technolog-
ical advancements throughout the African continent. Recognized as
the most powerful supercomputer in Africa and ranked 316th glob-
ally in the November 2024 Top500 report [31], Toubkal boasts an
exceptional computational performance exceeding 3.15 PFLOPS. Its
infrastructure features a robust set of general-purpose CPU nodes
capable of managing diverse workloads, high-memory nodes specif-
ically designed for data-intensive applications, and GPU-accelerated
nodes optimized for parallel processing tasks like machine-learning
and complex simulations (see Section 2 for more details).
These components are seamlessly interconnected via a high-
throughput, low-latency network fabric, facilitating rapid data
transfer and efficient communication across the system. This ad-
vanced infrastructure incorporates energy-efficient free-cooling
systems and is equipped with 1 MWp of solar panels, enabling it
to operate entirely on renewable energy during peak generation
periods. This commitment to sustainability not only enhances per-
formance but also aligns Toubkal with global efforts toward greener
computing solutions [27].
The Green500 [28] list ranks supercomputers according to their
energy efficiency, utilizing the metric of "performance per watt."
This metric quantifies the number of floating-point operations per
second (in GFLOPS) achieved for each watt of electrical power
demanded. By emphasizing performance per watt, the Green500
encourages sustainable practices within HPC. However, it is impor-
tant to note that this metric overlooks two significant factors: (1)

the contribution of on-site renewable energy sources and (2) the
role of energy management systems (EMS). EMS software solutions
are designed to optimize energy consumption across the infrastruc-
ture by exploiting for instance the DVFS technology [24–26]. A
more comprehensive evaluation of energy efficiency in supercom-
puters should consider these elements to better reflect their true
environmental impact.
In this paper, we present the methodology used to calculate the
energy efficiency metric for Toubkal, which contributed to an im-
pressive advancement of 174 places in the latest Green500 ranking
(from 336th in June 2024 to 162nd in November 2024). Additionally,
we emphasize the need for a reevaluation of the Green500 met-
ric, as it currently fails to account for the contributions of on-site
renewables and EMS optimizations. To highlight this issue, we con-
duct a series of benchmarks using two types of NVIDIA GPUs, the
A100 and H100, to demonstrate the potential for significant energy
savings through DVFS and without degrading performance.
This paper is structured as follows: Section 2 provides an overview
of the system’s components, including compute, high memory
(himem), GPU, frontend, and services. Section 3 details the soft-
ware stack of the Toubkal Supercomputer. Section 4 outlines the
methodology for assessing its energy efficiency. In Section 5, we
benchmark the A100 and H100 NVIDIA GPUs, highlighting the
advantages of DVFS. Finally, Section 6 offers concluding remarks.
2
System Description
Toubkal’s architecture includes several types of nodes, each opti-
mized for different computational tasks, as shown in Table 1. First,
we outline the Compute, Himem and GPU partitions, followed by
an overview of the Frontend and Service partitions.
2.1
Compute Partition
The Compute partition of the Toubkal Supercomputer consists of
1,272 nodes built on the Dell EMC PowerEdge C6420 architecture,
powered by Intel Xeon Platinum 8276L processors. Each node has
two sockets, each housing a 28-core CPU, resulting in a total of 56
cores per node, paired with 192 GB of memory. The theoretical peak
performance is approximately 5.01 PFLOPS, while the measured
performance with the Linpack benchmark is 3.16 PFLOPS.
2.2
Himem Partition
The Himem partition is specifically designed for applications re-
quiring large amounts of RAM. This partition consists of five nodes
based on the Dell PowerEdge R840 platform, each powered by four
Intel Xeon Platinum 8276L processors with 28 cores per CPU, and
each node features an impressive 1.5 Terabytes of RAM.
2.3
GPU Partitions
Toubkal’s GPU nodes, introduced in March 2022, include Dell Pow-
erEdge XE8545 servers with dual AMD EPYC 7713 processors (128
cores, 1TB RAM) and four NVIDIA A100-SXM4-80GB GPUs per
node. In March 2025, three additional PowerEdge XE8640 servers
were added, each with dual Intel Xeon Platinum 8468 processors
(96 cores, 1TB RAM) and four NVIDIA H100-HBM3-80GB GPUs.
All nodes are interconnected via a dual-rail Mellanox HDR200 In-
finiBand network, optimized for AI and ML workloads.
2.4
Frontend and Service Partitions
The Frontend of Toubkal serves as a versatile entry point for users,
enabling various activities such as software development, code
compilation, data management, job submission, data pre-processing
and post-processing, and result visualization. It consists of four
dedicated login nodes, which act as the primary access points to
the Toubkal system, allowing users to efficiently interact with both
computational resources and global filesystems.
Each login node is powered by dual Intel Xeon Platinum 8276
CPUs, providing a total of 56 logical processors (28 cores per CPU).
These high-end processors feature advanced capabilities and oper-
ate at a base frequency of 2.20 GHz, dynamically scaling from 1.0
GHz to a peak speed of 4.0 GHz depending on workload demands.
Additionally, the nodes are equipped with substantial cache mem-
ory, enhancing computational efficiency. Each processor includes
32 KB of L1d and L1i caches per core, 1 MB of L2 cache, and a total
of 39 MB of L3 cache. This hierarchical caching structure signifi-
cantly improves performance by enabling faster data retrieval. As
a result, the system delivers optimal efficiency across a wide range
of workloads, aligning with modern computational paradigms.
3
Software Ecosystem
Toubkal runs the Rocky Linux release 8.9 operating system on all
nodes and uses Slurm [36], a workload manager very popular for
most supercomputing installations. It also has several architecture-
specific software suites like Intel OneAPI and the NVIDIA HPC SDK
that give a comprehensive set of tools optimized to develop and
execute HPC applications. In addition, EasyBuild and Environment
Modules are used to simplify software administration and environ-
ment configuration, respectively, allowing flexibility in managing
software packages.
Furthermore, Toubkal has a broad set of HPC programming tools,
including both licensed and open-source solutions, and its software
environment is carefully designed to suit diverse research communi-
ties. It comes pre-installed with software specific to scientific fields
like chemistry, physics, deep learning, life and material science, and
meteorology, among others. This setup ensures efficiency and ease
of use for both the researcher and the developer by streamlining
handling related to the software environments.
The system includes fundamental computational research tools
such as compilers (GNU, Intel, NVIDIA), profilers and debuggers
(Valgrind, GDB, NVIDIA Nsight, CUDA-GDB), and communica-
tion libraries (OpenMPI, IntelMPI). Toubkal provides support for a
wide range of libraries and frameworks for numerical and scientific
applications, including LAPACK [2], OpenBLAS [35], MUMPS4PY
[15], PETSc [3], Eigen [12], FFTW [10] , and ParaView[1].
It also includes Python, Anaconda, MATLAB, and Ansys Fluent,
offering strong support for a variety of processes. For flexible envi-
ronment management, Toubkal has tools like Singularity [17] and
Apptainer [7]. System monitoring and health are managed using
the Open Monitoring Environment (OME) and XDMoD [21]. For
more details regarding software availability and configurations,
users can refer to the Toubkal user guide2 3.

Methodology
As established by the Green500 methodology [11], the energy effi-
ciency metric is defined as:

where 𝑃𝐻𝑃𝐿represents the peak performance achieved while exe-
cuting the high-performance Linpack (HPL) benchmark, measured
in gigaflops (GFLOPS). This metric captures the computational
power of the system. On the other hand, 𝐷𝐻𝑃𝐶signifies the maxi-
mum power demand of the whole HPC system, expressed in watts,
required to operate the HPL benchmark.
After Toubkal’s commissioning, no data regarding its maximum
demand was submitted to Green500, unlike the performance met-
ric reported to Top500, which was 3.16 PFLOPS. Consequently,
the energy efficiency metric derived from Equation (1) was calcu-
lated to be 0, resulting in Toubkal being categorized as one of the
least energy-efficient supercomputers in the world [32]. Toubkal’s
peak engineering power is designed to be 800 kW. With its Linpack
benchmark performance of 3.16 PFLOPS, we performed a mathemat-
ical analysis to recalculate the energy efficiency metric, yielding a
value of 3.16×106
800×103 = 3.95 GFLOPS/Watt. Furthermore, we compared
Toubkal with other similar systems listed on Green500 and iden-
tified several that were classified as more energy-efficient. Hence,
we re-ran the Linpack benchmark while closely monitoring the
demand of both the computing nodes and networking equipment.
Using our monitoring tools, we measured the power demand of
each node during HPL testing, which averaged 575 watts per node.
For our Top500 submission, Toubkal utilized 71,232 CPU cores,
equivalent to 1,272 nodes, each equipped with 56 cores, achieving
a measured HPL performance of 3.16 PFLOPS. In addition to the
power demand of the computing nodes, we also accounted for the
power demanded by the networking switches. Table 2 presents the
monitored power demand values for the 1,272 computing nodes as
well as 24 InfiniBand and 24 Ethernet switches. This data led to an
energy efficiency metric calculated at 3.16×106
754920 = 4.18 GFLOPS/Watt.
With these details submitted to Green500, Toubkal Supercomputer
secured the 162nd position in the latest November 2024 ranking
[29], improving 174 places.
From Equation (1), it’s evident that the simultaneous evaluation
of performance and power demand facilitates an assessment of en-
ergy efficiency in HPC systems. This approach emphasizes systems
that achieve exceptional performance while prioritizing energy
conservation, predominantly through the use of energy-efficient
hardware. However, it’s important to note that this metric does not

case of Toubkal) or the optimizations implemented, such as DVFS.
These factors can significantly influence the overall sustainability
impact of computing systems. Thus, we contend that the energy
efficiency metric of 4.18 GFLOPS/Watt for Toubkal does not ac-
curately represent its true energy efficiency, as it overlooks two
critical factors discussed earlier.
To complement the Green500 submission and evaluate addi-
tional factors influencing energy efficiency, we conducted a series
of experiments focused on GPU-based workloads and frequency
scaling. These experiments aim to assess the performance and en-
ergy trade-offs associated with different hardware configurations
and energy management strategies, specifically the comparison
between NVIDIA A100 and H100 GPUs, and the effect of DVFS on
core linear algebra operations, which are presented next.
5
Assessing Impact of Energy Management on
Performance
In this section, we explore the significance of energy management in
HPC systems, focusing on both GPU utilization and DVFS technolo-
gies. We start first by benchmarking A100 versus H100 to study the
performance-energy tradeoffs and then we consider different tradi-
tional governors and propose our ML-based one to demonstrate the
impact of energy management on this tradeoff. The benchmarks
are conducted across various numerical precisions, including FP16
(16-bit floating point), BF16 (Brain Floating Point 16-bit), TF32
(Tensor Float 32-bit), FP32 (32-bit float), FP64 (64-bit double pre-
cision), and TF64 (Tensor Float 64-bit), each offering a different
balance between computational speed and numerical accuracy.

5.1
Performance and Energy Efficiency: NVIDIA
A100 vs. H100 GPUs
To compare how GPU hardware affects energy efficiency, we bench-
marked the NVIDIA A100 and H100 GPUs across different preci-
sions and matrix dimensions through general matrix multiplication
(GEMM) [9] workloads. The metrics tracked were performance
(GFLOPS), power demand (Watts), execution time (milliseconds),
and energy used (Joules). These metrics were measured using the
cuBLAS library on a subset of Toubkal’s GPU nodes, with matrix
sizes ranging from 32 to 32,768 elements. Table 3 summarizes the
findings for a matrix size of 32,768 for both GPUs under identical
workloads, ensuring an equitable comparison. The H100 consis-
tently outperformed the A100 across all precisions, with notable
gains in lower-precision formats. Specifically, in FP16 precision,
the H100 achieved 655.132 TFLOPS compared to the A100’s 303.371
TFLOPS, resulting in a 2.16× speedup. In BF16 precision, the H100
reached 815.449 TFLOPS, a 2.79× speedup over the A100’s 291.917
TFLOPS. Similar performance advantages were also observed in
FP32, FP64, TF32, and TF64 precisions.
Despite the H100’s higher power draw (e.g., 14 W vs. 10 W for
A100 in FP16 and BF16), its energy consumption per operation was
lower due to significantly reduced execution times. For instance,
in BF16 at a matrix size of 32,768 elements, the H100 completed
GEMM 154.8 ms faster than the A100 (36% reduction), as shown
in Figure 2a. This efficiency is further illustrated in Figures 1a and
1b, where the H100’s higher power demand is offset by its superior
computational efficiency (e.g., speedup of x2).
The H100’s performance gains stem from enhanced tensor cores,
a higher clock speed (1980 MHz vs. 1410 MHz for A100), and HBM3
memory, aligning with findings from Databricks’ 2023 report on
LLM training with BF16 [20]. Figure 2b illustrates the significant
performance advantage of the H100 over the A100 in BF16 work-
loads, confirming the 2.79× speedup observed in Table 3. These
results suggest that upgrading Toubkal’s GPU infrastructure to
H100s could improve its energy efficiency metric beyond the cur-
rent 4.18 GFLOPS/Watt, particularly for workloads leveraging FP16
and BF16 precisions.
5.2
Optimizing GPU Frequency for Linear
Algebra Operations
In alignment with the energy efficiency metric set forth by Green500,
the previous section demonstrated that transitioning to more energy-
efficient hardware, such as the H100 in comparison to the A100, can
significantly improve overall energy efficiency. However, in this
section, we will delve into energy management strategies, thereby
reinforcing our initial assertion that the Green500’s energy effi-
ciency metric overlooks the critical aspect of energy management.
Specifically, we will examine how GPU clock frequency affects
the performance and power demand of fundamental linear algebra
operations. By employing DVFS technology alongside a machine
learning-based frequency prediction model, we sought to identify
optimal frequency ranges that strike a balance between perfor-
mance and power efficiency.

dug into how GPU clock frequency affects both performance and
energy use for some core linear algebra operations. We leaned on
cuBLAS for the math and NVIDIA’s Management Library (NVML)
to tweak the GPU frequencies, running tests based on workload-

5.2.3
Machine Learning-Based Frequency Prediction. To optimize
frequency generalization, we developed a machine learning model

5.3
Summary and Recommendations
Our findings provide several suggestions for designing energy-
efficient HPC systems that can improve Green500 rankings. First,
hardware selection matters: newer accelerators like the NVIDIA
H100 outperform the A100 in performance and energy consump-
tion, especially in low-precision workloads. Second, fixed-frequency
governors (e.g., performance or powersave) may not provide the
best energy-performance balance. Dynamic, workload-aware DVFS
strategies, like the ML-based predictor, consistently reduce energy
usage without compromising execution time, according to our ex-
periments.
Furthermore, our evaluation indicates that mid-range frequency
configurations (e.g., 1350-1980 MHz for GEMM FP16) are often more
efficient than extreme settings. Based on workload characteristics,
these results suggest system-level frequency tuning mechanism
integration. Beyond node-level optimization, energy-efficient HPC
design should include on-site renewable energy generation and ac-
curate power monitoring infrastructure, even though the Green500
metric does not yet account for them. These architectural elements
will improve sustainability and ranking performance as evaluation
criteria change.
6
Conclusion
In this paper, we evaluated the energy efficiency of the Toubkal Su-
percomputer, recently ranked 162nd on the November 2024 Green500
list with an energy efficiency metric of 4.18 GFLOPS/Watt. However,
we found this metric inadequate in fully capturing energy efficiency,
particularly regarding renewable energy use and dynamic energy
management strategies. Our comparison of the NVIDIA A100 and
H100 GPUs revealed that the H100 nearly doubled performance
and power efficiency under optimal workloads, achieving a 2.79x
speedup in the BF16 workload (see Table 3 and Figure 2b). This
suggests that upgrading the GPU infrastructure could significantly
enhance Toubkal’s power efficiency. Furthermore, our investigation
into GPU frequency optimization using LightGBM-based machine
learning identified optimal intermediate frequencies of 1350-1980
MHz for FP16 GEMM and 850-1350 MHz for FP64 GEMM, high-
lighting trade-offs between performance and energy consumption.
The findings suggest that Toubkal’s energy efficiency surpasses
the Green500 metric by considering additional elements such as the
presence of on-site renewable energy sources, cutting-edge GPU
hardware, and dynamic frequency scaling. Future research should
focus on evaluating the scalability of these optimizations across
Toubkal’s nodes, examining the effects of renewable energy inte-
gration on overall sustainability, and enhancing machine learning
models to forecast optimal frequencies for a broader spectrum of
workloads. These improvements would not only elevate Toubkal’s
position in the Green500 rankings but also support the overarching
objective of promoting energy-efficient HPC.

Abstract: Energy efficiency has emerged as a vital metric for evaluating high- performance computing (HPC) systems, often measured by the Green500 rankings using the "performance per watt" criterion. In this paper, we assess the energy efficiency of the Toubkal Super- computer based on the established Green500 metric. While we acknowledge the notable advancements in the rankings, we argue that the current energy efficiency metric for HPC systems adopted by the Green500 community overlooks two critical factors: the in- tegration of on-site renewable energy sources and the potential for energy management through dynamic frequency scaling of proces- sors. To support our argument, we consider GPU as well as dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS) technologies in a series of ex- periments. Utilizing our custom machine learning-based frequency predictor, our findings clearly illustrate the significant potential of energy management and DVFS to reduce energy consumption without compromising operational performance.
